si-emc-001.question: Which statement about the effective relative permittivity εeff of a microstrip line on a substrate of relative permittivity εr is correct?
choices: All of the electric field is confined inside the substrate, so it equals εr
Part of the electric field passes through the air, so it lies between 1 and εr
It is the sum of the relative permittivities of the substrate and the air, so it is εr + 1
si-emc-001.explanation: A microstrip has its signal trace on the surface of the substrate; most of the electric field between the trace and the ground on the back side passes through the substrate, but part of it passes through the air above. The propagation velocity is therefore set by an effective relative permittivity between air and substrate, εeff (1 < εeff < εr), with v = c/√εeff. The wider the trace, the more the field concentrates in the substrate, and εeff approaches εr. With two media, the wave is not pure TEM and is treated as quasi-TEM. A stripline, sandwiched between grounds above and below, is the case where all the field is in the dielectric and εeff = εr. εr + 1 simply adds the two.

si-emc-002.question: For a stripline in a dielectric with a relative permittivity of 4.0, which is closest to the time a signal takes to travel along a 10 cm trace? Take the speed of light as 3×10⁸ m/s.
choices: About 0.67 ns
About 0.33 ns
About 1.3 ns
si-emc-002.explanation: In a stripline all the electric field is in the dielectric, so the propagation velocity is v = c/√εr = 3×10⁸/2 = 1.5×10⁸ m/s. Traveling 10 cm takes 0.1/(1.5×10⁸) ≈ 0.67 ns, or about 67 ps per centimeter. About 0.33 ns ignores the dielectric and assumes the speed of light, and about 1.3 ns forgets the square root, computing c/εr. Length differences between the two traces of a differential pair, or length variations across a parallel bus, become differences in this propagation time and cause skew, so trace lengths are matched.

si-emc-003.question: Approximating a digital signal with a 100 ps rise time (10% to 90%) by a first-order low-pass response, what is the guideline bandwidth (from BW ≈ 0.35/tr)?
choices: About 35 GHz
About 10 GHz
About 3.5 GHz
si-emc-003.explanation: In a first-order low-pass system, the rise time tr and the −3 dB bandwidth BW are related by BW ≈ 0.35/tr. For tr = 100 ps = 1×10⁻¹⁰ s, 0.35/10⁻¹⁰ = 3.5×10⁹ Hz, about 3.5 GHz. About 35 GHz is an order-of-magnitude error treating 100 ps as 10⁻¹¹ s, and about 10 GHz uses 1/tr, forgetting the coefficient. Even if the signal repeats at a low frequency, a fast edge contains frequency components of this order, so traces, probes and oscilloscopes must also handle this bandwidth. The 0.35 coefficient assumes a first-order system.

si-emc-004.question: Two lines, each with a characteristic impedance of 50 Ω, are spaced far enough apart that their coupling is negligible and used as a differential pair. What is the differential impedance?
si-emc-004.explanation: In differential signaling, opposite currents flow in the two lines, and the differential impedance is the voltage between them (the differential voltage) divided by that current. Without coupling, each line is 50 Ω and the two appear in series, so Zdiff = 2 × 50 = 100 Ω. 25 Ω is the two in parallel, corresponding to the common-mode impedance with currents flowing in the same direction in both. Bringing the lines closer couples them and makes the differential impedance less than 2Z0, so when a tightly coupled 100 Ω differential pair is designed, each line's single-ended impedance is set somewhat above 50 Ω.

si-emc-005.question: When considering unwanted radiation (EMI) from cables, which is the correct reason common-mode current on a cable is a particular problem?
choices: Common-mode current is the current that carries the signal itself, so reducing it stops the signal from reaching the receiver
Common-mode current is a DC component, so it hardly ever makes the cable radiate high-frequency electromagnetic waves
The outgoing and return currents do not cancel, so even a small current makes the whole cable radiate as an antenna
si-emc-005.explanation: In differential mode, equal and opposite currents flow close together on the outgoing and return paths, so at a distance their radiation almost cancels. In common mode, currents flow in the same direction on both lines (or on the whole cable including the shield), and the return path goes through distant ground or the chassis, so there is no cancellation and the whole cable becomes a long antenna. As a result, a common-mode current much smaller than the differential-mode current can produce comparable radiation. Common-mode current is not needed to transmit the signal, so it can be reduced with ferrite cores or common-mode chokes.

si-emc-006.question: Which statement about crosstalk between two parallel traces in a stripline in a homogeneous dielectric is correct?
choices: Far-end crosstalk (FEXT) cancels between inductive and capacitive coupling and is ideally almost zero
Near-end crosstalk (NEXT) grows without limit, in proportion to length, as the parallel section gets longer
Widening the spacing between traces lowers the mutual capacitance but, conversely, raises the mutual inductance, so crosstalk increases
si-emc-006.explanation: Crosstalk arises from coupling through the mutual inductance and mutual capacitance with the neighboring line. At the far end (the side traveling in the same direction as the signal), the two contributions have opposite signs, and in a homogeneous medium they are equal in size, so they cancel and FEXT is almost zero. In microstrip, part of the field is in the air, which upsets the balance, so FEXT remains. Near-end crosstalk saturates at a constant value once the round-trip propagation time of the parallel section exceeds the rise time, and making the section longer does not increase it further. Wider spacing weakens the coupling and reduces crosstalk.

si-emc-007.question: Which is closest to the skin depth of copper (resistivity 1.7×10⁻⁸ Ω·m, permeability equal to that of vacuum, 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m) at 100 MHz? Take the skin depth as δ = √(ρ/(πfμ)).
choices: About 6.6 µm
About 66 µm
About 0.66 mm
si-emc-007.explanation: πfμ = π × 10⁸ × 4π×10⁻⁷ ≈ 395, so δ = √(1.7×10⁻⁸/395) ≈ √(4.3×10⁻¹¹) ≈ 6.6×10⁻⁶ m, about 6.6 µm. About 66 µm is the value at 1 MHz and about 0.66 mm at 10 kHz; skin depth is inversely proportional to the square root of frequency, so 100 times the frequency gives 1/10 the depth. RF current concentrates within roughly one skin depth of the conductor surface, so even a thick conductor has a small effective cross section and higher resistance. That is why surface roughness and the plating material of conductors have a large effect on loss.

si-emc-008.question: At frequencies where the skin effect is fully developed, how do the skin depth and RF resistance of a conductor change roughly when the frequency is quadrupled?
choices: The skin depth falls to 1/4 and the resistance quadruples
The skin depth halves and the resistance doubles
The skin depth doubles and the resistance halves
si-emc-008.explanation: The skin depth δ = √(ρ/(πfμ)) is inversely proportional to the square root of frequency, so four times the frequency gives √4 = 2, halving it. With the current-carrying thickness halved, the conductor's RF resistance roughly doubles; it increases in proportion to √f. 1/4 and 4 times forget the square root, and the skin depth doubles when the frequency is cut to 1/4. As a result, the conductor loss of a transmission line (in dB/m) increases as √f, and combined with dielectric loss, which increases in proportion to frequency, trace loss rises sharply at high frequencies.

si-emc-009.question: In TDR (time-domain reflectometry), a reflection is observed 2.0 ns after the step is launched. If the propagation velocity of the line is 1.5×10⁸ m/s, how far away is the discontinuity?
choices: 30 cm
60 cm
15 cm
si-emc-009.explanation: The time observed in TDR is the round-trip time for the step to reach the discontinuity and come back. The distance is d = v·t/2 = 1.5×10⁸ × 2.0×10⁻⁹/2 = 0.15 m, or 15 cm. 30 cm forgets the round trip and uses v·t, and 60 cm uses the speed of light (3×10⁸ m/s) and also forgets the round trip. The propagation velocity is set by the dielectric of the board or cable, so you need to know εeff or the velocity factor to get an accurate distance. In this way TDR can locate connectors, vias and breaks from the timing.

si-emc-010.question: Looking at a TDR waveform in a 50 Ω system, the waveform steps up at a certain position. What can be said about the line impedance at that position?
choices: It is lower than 50 Ω
It equals 50 Ω and is matched
It is higher than 50 Ω
si-emc-010.explanation: In TDR, the reflection coefficient at each position, Γ = (Z − Z0)/(Z + Z0), appears as a step in the waveform. When Z is higher than Z0, Γ is positive, the reflected wave adds to the incident step and the waveform rises, so this position is higher than 50 Ω. An open end gives Γ = +1 and doubles the voltage, and a short gives Γ = −1 and drops it to zero. Lower than Z0 makes the waveform fall, and a match produces no step. A local capacitance (such as a large pad) shows as a downward dip and a local inductance (such as a bond wire) as an upward bump, so you can see where the trace departs from its design value.

si-emc-011.question: In the eye diagram of a 10 Gb/s NRZ signal, the total (peak-to-peak) jitter is 30 ps. Which is closest to the horizontal eye opening (consider no factor other than jitter)?
choices: 70 ps
100 ps
40 ps
si-emc-011.explanation: The time for one bit (UI) at 10 Gb/s is 1/(10×10⁹) = 100 ps. The left and right crossing points are each spread over a total width of 30 ps by jitter, half of which eats into the eye on each side, so the horizontal opening is 100 − 30 = 70 ps (eye width = 1 UI − total jitter). 100 ps is the UI itself without jitter. 40 ps double-counts, subtracting the total jitter at both the left and right crossings. In real evaluations, the distribution of random jitter has long tails, so the jitter is estimated as the width corresponding to the target bit error rate (for example, 10⁻¹²).

si-emc-012.question: Which material is best for shielding low-frequency magnetic fields below a few kHz (for example, leakage flux from a power transformer)?
choices: Thin foil of a good conductor such as copper or aluminum
A high-permeability magnetic material such as permalloy
A plastic case coated with conductive paint
si-emc-012.explanation: At low frequencies the skin depth of conductors is large (about 2.6 mm for aluminum at 1 kHz), and eddy currents in a thin conductor do little to cancel the magnetic field. Instead, high-permeability permalloy or silicon steel is used to provide a path for the flux and divert it around the part to be protected. Aluminum foil and conductive paint are effective shields against electric fields and high-frequency electromagnetic waves through reflection and absorption, but they do little against low-frequency magnetic fields. Shielding materials are chosen according to whether the field is electric or magnetic and what its frequency is.

si-emc-013.question: Which statement about electromagnetic leakage through a long, narrow gap (a slot) in a metal enclosure is correct?
choices: The amount of leakage is set only by the area of the opening, not by its shape, whether long and thin or round
When the slot length approaches half a wavelength, it resonates as an antenna and leaks heavily even if its area is small
If the gap is narrow enough, leakage is negligible even if its length exceeds half a wavelength
si-emc-013.explanation: A slot acts as a slot antenna, complementary to a metal plate (dipole) of the same shape. When its length is close to half a wavelength, it resonates and radiates efficiently, so even a thin gap of small area can be a major source of leakage. At 1 GHz, for example, half a wavelength is 15 cm, and long gaps such as lid seams easily reach that length. Shielding performance is therefore set by the largest dimension of an opening rather than its area, and long gaps are broken into short sections by tightening the screw spacing or adding gaskets. For the same area, a vent made of many small holes leaks less than a single long slot.

si-emc-014.question: Which is closest to the self-resonant frequency of a multilayer ceramic capacitor with a capacitance of 10 nF and an equivalent series inductance (ESL) of 0.5 nH?
choices: About 450 MHz
About 7.1 MHz
About 71 MHz
si-emc-014.explanation: A capacitor can be treated as a series resonant circuit of the capacitance C and the ESL, with a self-resonant frequency f = 1/(2π√(LC)). √(0.5×10⁻⁹ × 10×10⁻⁹) = √(5×10⁻¹⁸) ≈ 2.24×10⁻⁹ s, so f ≈ 1/(2π × 2.24×10⁻⁹) ≈ 71 MHz. About 450 MHz forgets to divide by 2π, and about 7.1 MHz is the value for a capacitance 100 times larger (1 µF). Above its self-resonant frequency, a capacitor behaves as an inductor, and its impedance rises with frequency. To keep decoupling effective at high frequencies, use capacitors with low ESL and also reduce the inductance of the traces and vias to power and ground.

si-emc-015.question: Which is the correct reason a slit in the ground plane crossing beneath a high-speed signal trace is a problem?
choices: High-frequency return current tries to flow right under the trace, so the slit forces a detour that enlarges the loop and increases reflection and radiation
The DC resistance of the ground increases, lowering the DC level of the signal enough to fall below the logic threshold
The slit makes the signal propagate faster than light, so it reaches the receiving end early and the timing shifts
si-emc-015.explanation: At high frequencies, the return current concentrates on the path of minimum loop inductance, that is, in the plane directly beneath the signal trace. If there is a slit right under the trace, the return current must detour around the end of the slit, increasing the current loop area. As a result, the inductance there increases, creating an impedance discontinuity that causes reflections, and radiation from the loop and crosstalk with other traces also increase. At DC the current spreads over the whole plane, so the slit lowers the DC level very little; that is not the essence of the problem. Nor does the propagation velocity exceed the speed of light.

si-emc-016.question: Which statement about how the loss of a printed circuit board trace behaves as frequency is raised is correct? Assume the loss tangent tanδ is nearly independent of frequency.
choices: Dielectric loss is constant with frequency and conductor loss grows as f², so at higher frequencies only conductor loss matters
Both conductor and dielectric loss grow in proportion to f, so their ratio is the same at every frequency and does not change with the materials
Conductor loss goes roughly as √f due to the skin effect and dielectric loss as f, so at high enough frequencies dielectric loss dominates
si-emc-016.explanation: The high-frequency resistance of a conductor is inversely proportional to the skin depth δ ∝ 1/√f, so conductor loss (dB/m) is roughly proportional to √f. Dielectric loss, by contrast, loses an energy per wavelength set by tanδ, so per unit length it is proportional to frequency: α ≈ πf√εeff·tanδ/c [Np/m]. As a result, the share of dielectric loss increases on higher-frequency traces, and switching from FR-4 (tanδ ≈ 0.02) to a low-loss material with tanδ around 0.002 pays off more. In practice, copper surface roughness makes conductor loss grow faster than √f as well, so smooth copper foils are also used. Calling it f², or saying the ratio is constant, is wrong.

si-emc-017.question: A via that changes layers in a board leaves an unused portion (stub) 1.5 mm long that carries no signal, in a dielectric with a relative permittivity of 4.0. Which frequency is closest to where this open-ended stub resonates at λ/4 and creates a deep notch in the transmission? Take the speed of light as 3×10⁸ m/s.
choices: 25 GHz
50 GHz
12.5 GHz
si-emc-017.explanation: The frequency at which the stub is a quarter wavelength long is f = c/(4L√εr) = 3×10⁸/(4 × 1.5×10⁻³ × 2.0) = 2.5×10¹⁰ Hz, or 25 GHz. A λ/4 stub with an open end looks like a short at its base, so it strongly attenuates signals at that frequency. 50 GHz forgets √εr, and 12.5 GHz uses εr itself instead of √εr. Because 25 GHz is near the Nyquist frequency of signals at tens of Gb/s, high-speed designs shorten the stub by back-drilling the unused part of the via or by choosing layers that leave no stub.

si-emc-018.question: For a circuit with a 1.0 V supply, an allowed voltage variation of ±3%, and a maximum load current change of 10 A, which value is closest to the target impedance of the power distribution network (PDN), defined as allowed voltage variation ÷ current change?
choices: 30 mΩ
3 mΩ
si-emc-018.explanation: The allowed voltage variation is 1.0 V × 0.03 = 30 mV, so the target impedance is 30 mV/10 A = 3 mΩ. 30 mΩ takes 3% as 0.3, an error of one order of magnitude, and 0.1 Ω divides the supply voltage itself by the current. The PDN impedance seen from the load must stay below this value up to frequencies matching how fast the current changes. The voltage regulator module (VRM) covers the lowest frequencies, bulk capacitors the next range, multilayer ceramic capacitors the range above, and package and on-chip capacitance together with the power and ground planes the highest. It is also important that the parallel-resonance (antiresonance) peaks between capacitors do not exceed the target.

si-emc-019.question: What does a common-mode choke at the end of a cable (a coil in which two wires are wound together in the same sense on a ferrite core) do?
choices: It presents a large impedance only to the differential signal current to cut high-frequency components, while passing common-mode current straight through to ground
It increases the capacitance between the two wires to slow the rise of the differential signal, reducing the signal's high-frequency content itself to suppress radiation
Differential current flows in opposite directions, so its fluxes cancel and the choke barely acts, while common-mode current flowing the same way sees a large impedance
si-emc-019.explanation: With the two wires wound in the same sense, differential current flows in opposite directions on the go and return wires, so the fluxes in the core cancel and the inductance hardly acts. Common-mode current flows in the same direction on both wires, so the fluxes add and present a large inductance (and, at high frequencies, a resistive part from ferrite loss) that reduces the current. The choke can therefore suppress just the common-mode current, the main cause of cable radiation, while barely affecting the signal waveform. Saying it acts only on differential current is backwards. Adding capacitance between the wires is not what a choke does, and slowing the rise time would also degrade signal quality.

si-emc-020.question: On a circuit board, which statement about the radiated electric field from the small loop formed by the outgoing and return signal currents (differential mode) is correct? Assume the loop is much smaller than a wavelength.
choices: It scales with current, loop area, and frequency squared, so routing the return path right beside the signal line to shrink the area cuts radiation
The outgoing and return currents are equal and opposite, so the radiation cancels completely regardless of loop area and is always zero
It is proportional only to the current magnitude regardless of frequency, so high-frequency harmonics of the signal radiate as strongly as the fundamental
si-emc-020.explanation: A small loop acts as a magnetic dipole antenna, and its far-field radiated electric field is roughly proportional to f²·A·I (f the frequency, A the loop area, I the current). Even though the outgoing and return currents are opposite, the two wires are separated, so the cancellation is incomplete, and what remains is proportional to the area. Because it grows with the square of frequency, harmonics of fast-edged signals radiate more readily. The basic remedy is to place a ground plane directly under the signal line so the return current flows close by and the loop area is small. Saying it cancels to zero, or that it does not depend on frequency, is wrong. Common-mode radiation from cables, by contrast, is proportional to frequency and cable length.
